title: Strongly inert-active matching and the operadic base filtration
statement:
Use simplicial sets and nerves of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones], finite pointed maps, and the active/inert conventions of [def-coef-symmetric-operadic-family] and [lem-coef-operadic-approximation-restriction]. Fix $m\geq2$ and put $B_+=N(\mathrm{Fin}_*)\times\Delta^{\{1,\ldots,m\}}$ and $B=N(\mathrm{Fin}_*)\times\Delta^m$. Write $\langle s\rangle=\{*,1,\ldots,s\}$. A base arrow is strongly inert if its simplex coordinate is constant, its pointed map is inert and the injection of the nonbasepoint fibers is increasing; it is active if its pointed map has preimage of the basepoint equal to the basepoint, and neutral if neither. Every base arrow has a unique factorization as strongly inert followed by active. Call a nondegenerate chain new if its coordinate image contains all $1,\ldots,m$, and closed if its final arity is $1$.
The new nondegenerate chains have the following exhaustive, disjoint matching classification. In the two neutral classes an arbitrary prefix of earlier edges is permitted; no such prefix is implicit in the active-seed or output classes. Active seeds are closed all-active chains. A shorter neutral chain has a neutral arrow followed by an active block (possibly empty) and then a strongly inert tail (possibly empty). Its unique longer partner replaces that neutral arrow by its strongly-inert/active factorization. Conversely a longer neutral chain has a distinguished strongly inert arrow followed by a nonempty active block and then a strongly inert tail; deleting the intervening factorization vertex, a strictly inner vertex, gives the shorter chain. A shorter output chain is open and consists of an active block followed by a strongly inert tail, either block possibly empty. If its final arity is $s>0$, its longer output partners are exactly the $s$ chains obtained by appending a color projection $\langle s\rangle\to\langle1\rangle$; deleting the last vertex gives the shorter chain. The longer output chains are precisely the closed chains with an active block followed by a nonempty strongly inert tail. A shorter output chain with final arity zero has no partner and is called a nullary seed. Each new chain belongs to exactly one of the active-seed, shorter-neutral, longer-neutral, shorter-output or longer-output classes; the nullary seeds form the indicated subset of the shorter-output class.
For $k\geq0$, let $F_k\subseteq B_+$ be generated by $N(\mathrm{Fin}_*)\times\partial\Delta^{\{1,\ldots,m\}}$, all nondegenerate simplices of dimension $<k$, and the $k$-dimensional longer partners of both kinds. Let $\widehat F_k\subseteq B$ consist of simplices whose strictly positive-coordinate block belongs to $F_k$, allowing an arbitrary initial coordinate-zero block and allowing the positive block to be empty. Then $\widehat F_0=N(\mathrm{Fin}_*)\times\Lambda_0^m$, the $\widehat F_k$ increase, and $\bigcup_k\widehat F_k=B$. For $k>0$, $F_k$ is generated over $F_{k-1}$ by active seeds and nullary seeds of dimension $k-1$, and the shorter chains of dimension $k-1$ together with all their longer partners. For $k>0$ the nondegenerate simplices of $F_k$ not in $F_{k-1}$ are exactly the active seeds, nullary seeds and shorter chains of dimension $k-1$ and the longer partners of dimension $k$. For every simplicial map $u:M\to B$ put $M(k)=u^{-1}(\widehat F_k)=M\times_B\widehat F_k$. Then $M(0)=M\times_B(N(\mathrm{Fin}_*)\times\Lambda_0^m)$, $M(k-1)\subseteq M(k)$, $\bigcup_kM(k)=M$, and for $k>0$ a simplex $x$ of $M$ lies in $M(k)$ but not in $M(k-1)$ exactly when the positive-coordinate block of $u(x)$ is nonempty and is a degeneracy of an active seed, a nullary seed or a shorter chain of dimension $k-1$, or of a longer partner of dimension $k$; the initial coordinate-zero block of $u(x)$ is arbitrary. No claim is made that inverse image commutes with simplicial generation. This statement supplies a classification and domains, with no map into a target category and no target extension conclusion.

source.place: Proof of Theorem 3.1.2.3, printed pp.334-335 and step (2), p.337: normal form, five matching classes and F(k); the inconsistent printed G(2)/G(3) labels are replaced by semantic names. This is the classification and filtration hidden in returned parent step 4. September 18, 2017 edition read online; shared archival copy WANTED. No Stacks tag states this quasicategorical assertion.

proof.text: For a pointed map $\alpha:\langle r\rangle\to\langle s\rangle$, let $D=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,r\}:\alpha(i)\ne *\}$. Order $D$ increasingly and let $e:\langle |D|\rangle\to D_+$ be the unique pointed bijection that is increasing on nonbasepoints. Define $\rho:\langle r\rangle\to\langle |D|\rangle$ by sending the $j$th element of $D$ to $j$ and every other input to $*$, and define $\beta:\langle |D|\rangle\to\langle s\rangle$ by $\beta(j)=\alpha(e(j))$. Then $\rho$ is inert, its nonbasepoint fibers occur in increasing order, and $\beta^{-1}(*)=\{*\}$, so $\beta$ is active; moreover $\alpha=\beta\rho$. If $\alpha=\beta'\rho'$ is another factorization with the same properties, the nonbasepoint inputs retained by $\rho'$ are exactly $D$, and increasing order forces its intermediate pointed set and $\rho'$ to be the displayed ones; then $\beta'=\beta$. Thus every base arrow has a unique strongly-inert/active factorization. The definition of active and inert used here is the pointed-map definition in [lem-coef-operadic-approximation-restriction].

source.place: Proof of Theorem 3.1.2.3, normal-form paragraph, printed p.334; finite pointed-set factorization expanded from the stated active/inert definitions.

proof.text: A simplex of $B_+$ is a chain of pointed maps together with a weakly increasing simplex-coordinate chain, by the nerve description. Remove degeneracies using the unique nondegenerate-simplex decomposition [lem-weil-pbc-simplicial-set-nondegenerate-decomposition]. On a nondegenerate chain, factor each pointed-map edge by Step 1 and record the resulting word in the alphabet $S$ (strongly inert), $A$ (active), and $N$ (neither). The simplex coordinate is weakly increasing along the chain, constant along strongly inert edges, and the chain is new exactly when its coordinate image contains every positive coordinate $1,\ldots,m$. The final arity and whether the final pointed set has one nonbasepoint define the closed/open distinction. Since the factorization at each edge is unique, these normal-form words and the positions of their vertices are intrinsic, so any later case distinction is disjoint. In the nerve of the product category $\mathrm{Fin}_*\times[m-1]$ a simplex is nondegenerate exactly when no edge is an identity in both coordinates; an edge that is both strongly inert and active has inert increasing bijective pointed map, hence the identity, and constant coordinate, so it does not occur, and every edge of a nondegenerate chain receives exactly one letter.

source.place: Proof of Theorem 3.1.2.3, normal-form paragraph, printed p.334; nerve/simplex conventions and nondegenerate-chain reduction.

proof.text: Scan a new nondegenerate chain in its unique normal form and let $T$ be its longest suffix whose word is an active block followed by a strongly-inert block, i.e. an $A^*S^*$ suffix. If there is a letter immediately before $T$, classify the chain by that letter (with the earlier edges forming the permitted neutral prefix). If that letter is neutral, the chain is shorter-neutral: after the distinguished neutral edge all remaining edges are exactly the $A^*S^*$ suffix. If that letter is strongly inert and the $A$-block in $T$ is nonempty, the chain is longer-neutral. This longest-suffix rule handles words such as $NSA$ and $NN$, where the first neutral edge would give the wrong classification. If there is no preceding letter, the whole word is $A^*S^*$; the chain is an open output chain unless it is closed with a nonempty strongly-inert tail, in which case it is a longer output chain, while the closed all-active case is the active seed. These alternatives are exhaustive because every edge is exactly one of strongly inert, active, or neutral, and they are disjoint by the unique longest $A^*S^*$ suffix, its preceding letter, and the final arity.

source.place: Proof of Theorem 3.1.2.3, five matching classes, printed pp.334-335; semantic active-seed, neutral, and output cases.

proof.text: For a shorter-neutral chain, factor its distinguished neutral arrow as the unique strongly-inert arrow followed by the unique active arrow from Step 1. Insert the intermediate vertex. This produces a longer chain whose new vertex is strictly inner, and deleting that vertex recovers the shorter chain. Every longer-neutral chain has, by the longest-suffix scan in Step 3, a unique distinguished strongly-inert arrow immediately before a nonempty active block and then a strongly-inert tail; deleting the vertex between that distinguished factor and the active block gives the inverse shorter chain. The inserted/deleted vertex is inner because the distinguished factorization lies before the nonempty suffix block, and uniqueness of Step 1 makes the two operations inverse. Hence shorter-neutral and longer-neutral chains form disjoint pairs with the asserted unique matching face.

source.place: Proof of Theorem 3.1.2.3, neutral matching, printed p.335.

proof.text: For an open output chain with final arity $s>0$, append one of the $s$ color projections $\langle s\rangle\to\langle1\rangle$. Each appended projection is strongly inert, and its choice is exactly the chosen nonbasepoint of $\langle s\rangle$, so the resulting chains are distinct. Deleting the final vertex reverses the construction, hence these are exactly the longer output partners and the deleted face is the last face. A chain obtained this way is closed and has an active block followed by a nonempty strongly-inert tail. Conversely every closed chain with such a tail has a unique last projection in its strongly-inert tail; deleting its last vertex gives the corresponding open chain, and the final arity identifies one of the $s$ projections. When $s=0$ there is no color projection, so the shorter chain has no partner and is precisely a nullary seed. This proves the shorter-output/longer-output classification and the stated nullary subfamily.

source.place: Proof of Theorem 3.1.2.3, output matching, printed pp.335-336.

proof.text: Filter $B_+$ by nondegenerate dimension and by the preceding matching. The boundary-coordinate simplices are present at every stage. At stage $0$, allowing an arbitrary initial zero-coordinate block and an empty positive block gives exactly the $0$th horn $N(\mathrm{Fin}_*)\times\Lambda_0^m$: a positive-coordinate simplex lies in it exactly when its coordinate image omits at least one of $1,\ldots,m$. For $k>0$, the dimension-$(k-1)$ active and nullary seeds enter $F_k$ through the clause containing all nondegenerate simplices of dimension $<k$. The dimension-$(k-1)$ longer partners already lie in $F_{k-1}$. The remaining dimension-$(k-1)$ new chains are the shorter members of the two matching pairs, and their dimension-$k$ longer partners are the additional generators; no nondegenerate simplex of dimension $k$ lies in $F_{k-1}$, whose generators have dimension at most $k-1$, and no seed or shorter chain of dimension $k-1$ lies in $F_{k-1}$, since it is new, is not a longer partner, and the faces of the generators of dimension $k-1$ have dimension at most $k-2$. Hence the nondegenerate simplices of $F_k\setminus F_{k-1}$ are exactly the listed ones; the preceding case analysis proves there are no other possibilities. Thus adjoining those seeds and matched pairs to $F_{k-1}$ gives $F_k$. Since every nondegenerate simplex has finite dimension, the increasing union of the $F_k$ is all of $B_+$. Adding arbitrary initial zero-coordinate blocks gives the same assertions for $\widehat F_k\subseteq B$, including $\widehat F_0=N(\mathrm{Fin}_*)\times\Lambda_0^m$.

source.place: Proof of Theorem 3.1.2.3, definition of $F(k)$ and step (2), printed p.337.

proof.text: Let $u:M\to B$ be any simplicial map. Pullback of a simplicial subset is degreewise, and every face or degeneracy of a simplex is obtained by applying the corresponding operator to its chain. The normal-form factorization, the longest $A^*S^*$ suffix and its preceding letter, the final arity, and the chosen color projection are all computed in the target chain $u(\sigma)$; therefore the five classes and their matching faces pull back to the inverse images of the same classes. The inclusions $F_{k-1}\subseteq F_k$, the unions over $k$, and the degreewise differences between successive stages are preserved by inverse image. A simplex of $B$ lies in $\widehat F_k\setminus\widehat F_{k-1}$ exactly when its positive block lies in $F_k\setminus F_{k-1}$; since $F_k$ and $F_{k-1}$ are simplicial subsets, by the unique nondegenerate decomposition a simplex lies in one of them exactly when its nondegenerate root does, so this positive block is a degeneracy of one of the nondegenerate simplices listed in step 6. Applying this to $u(x)$ gives the stated description of $M(k)\setminus M(k-1)$; no assertion that inverse image commutes with simplicial generation is needed. In particular the arbitrary initial coordinate-zero blocks remain arbitrary after pullback, and the filtration and its degreewise stage description hold for $u^{-1}(F_k)$ and $u^{-1}(\widehat F_k)$.

reviewed.note: mechanical checks by tools/merge_delivery.py; mathematics reviewed in full by NT-cc-Q131-bdac76e12 (reviewer sub-agent of L); spot-checked: I read the item in full: its 7 steps, the cited statements (approximation-restriction for the inert/active definitions, def-cbc for nerves and horns, the nondegenerate-decomposition Mathlib leaf, def-coef-symmetric-operadic-family) and its only citer, left-horn-filling, where step 4 uses the item and steps 5-9 use the result. HA Thm 3.1.2.3 is not in literature/: the worker filed it as WANTED, and proof_origin=agent is correct. I checked every claim by hand on finite pointed sets instead. (1) The strongly-inert/active factorization exists and is strictly unique. (2) An edge that is both strongly inert and active is degenerate, so the S/A/N letters partition the edges of a nondegenerate chain. (3) Neutral matching: both factors are nondegenerate, the composite of a strongly-inert edge with an active edge is neutral, and the longest-A*S*-suffix rule is preceded by S or N, never A; tested on NSA, NN, SA, NA, SSA and AS. (4) Output matching: a closed A*S+ chain has s>=2, the shorter chain is still new, and s=0 gives the nullary seed. (5) The positive block lies in F_0 exactly when the simplex lies in N(Fin_*)xLambda_0^m. (6) Each widehat F_k is a simplicial subset, the stages increase, and their union is B. There are no new nodes and no duplicates (rg for strongly inert, seeds, 3.1.2.3 and factorization; inert-active-factorization, family-cell-presentation and inert-factor-equivalence differ). The route stays inside sk-prop-sf-biduality-general, so there are no tool_uses. There is no SGA citation, and no coefficient category or base change is involved. Three repairable faults, fixed in fixes/dag/nodes/sec-six-functors/lem-coef-symmetric-operadic-base-matching.json: (a) step 2 said 'The coordinate is constant on B_+', which is false; corrected, and the letter-partition argument is added. (b) Step 6 left out the dimension-(k-1) longer partners already in F_{k-1} and did not check that the generators are new; completed. (c) The statement said 'These assertions remain true after inverse image along any simplicial map', which is false if read as generation. Counterexample: Delta^k->Delta^{k-1}->B through a seed; the top simplex of M is in M(k) minus M(k-1) but is not generated. I replaced it with the exact degreewise description: x is in M(k) minus M(k-1) exactly when the positive block of u(x) is a degeneracy of a seed or shorter chain of dimension k-1, or of a longer partner of dimension k. This is what step 7 actually proves and what the citer uses. Step 7 now cites the nondegenerate-decomposition leaf, which was already in proof_deps.
